newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No new jobs in Australian manufacturing - report.
newsitem.headline: No new jobs in Australian manufacturing - report.

text.p: Australians, facing a stubbornly high unemployment rate, should not look to the manufacturing industry to provide new jobs, an economics consultancy said on Wednesday.
Access Economics said manufacturing was unlikely to provide new jobs as it could increase output without boosting employment levels.

In its July Economics Monitor, Access said productivity in Australian manufacturing lagged so far behind the rest of the world that output could rise by more than 60 percent without any labour increases.
"Improving the productivity performance of manufacturing would mean producing more with fewer inputs of labour and capital," Access said.
"If Australian manufacturing moves closer to world best practice this suggests that manufacturing is unlikely to produce many new jobs in aggregate," Access said.
Australia's unemployment rate has been stuck above 8.5 percent since Prime Minister John Howard's conservative Liberal-National coalition government was elected in March 1996.
Unemployment rose to 8.8 percent in May and economists are expecting the jobless rate to be 8.7 percent in June.
However, Access said improving manufacturing productivity would result in higher incomes in the industry and more jobs in service industries where those incomes would be spent.
"The challenge for individual manufacturing firms is to identify how much they are lagging best practice, the causes and how to close the gap," it said.
Access said labour market reforms were central to closing the productivity gap, but the reforms needed to improve work practices as well as allow lower minimum wages.
Howard said on Tuesday there was no need to change minimum wage levels to combat unemployment, but stressed that the community needed to understand the impact wages had on jobs.
He has called a special cabinet meeting for August to discuss unemployment and ways of reducing the high jobless rate.
Access said the challenge facing the government was to clearly spell out the likely benefits from continued change in manufacturing industry, while making sure the reform process did not falter.
"While Australian productivity may have improved substantially in recent years, we started well behind best practice," it said.
"Moreover, productivity is also continuously improving overseas so we have not been closing the gap.
"If 'reform fatigue' sets in, Australia will rapidly slip even further behind," Access said.
